Article Monetary Dynamics and Inflation Persistence: A Machine Learning Approach Applied to Turkey Ibrahim Bakirtas 1,* , Muhammed Rasid Bakir 2 and Gokay Canberk Bulus 1 1 Department of Economics, Faculty of Economics and Administrative Sciences, Aksaray University, 68100 Aksaray, Turkey; gcbulus@aksaray.edu.tr 2 Office of Quality Coordination, Aksaray University, 68100 Aksaray, Turkey; mrasidbakir@aksaray.edu.tr * Correspondence: ibakirtas@aksaray.edu.tr Abstract This study re-assesses the root causes of inflation through an innovative hybrid analytical framework integrating deep neural networks, random forest algorithms, and causal infer- ence (DoWhy) within the Quantity-Theoretical Inflation Theory, using monthly data from Turkey for the period 2003M05–2025M01. The findings reveal that inflation expectations and exchange rate fluctuations are the most influential drivers of inflation, overshadowing other variables such as money supply, real interest rates, and global oil prices. Although the exact ordering of predictors is model dependent, and the random forest assigns the leading role to the real interest rate, the signal shared across all three methodological pathways rests on expectations and the exchange rate. While money supply growth aligns with monetarist theory and remains a consistent source of upward price pressure, its impact is often mediated through expectations and currency depreciation. Causal estimates confirm that Turkey’s persistent inflation is fueled not just by macroeconomic imbalances but by the erosion of policy credibility and weak anchoring of expectations, particularly after 2017. The study contributes methodologically by introducing AI-powered modeling to inflation analysis in emerging markets, and empirically by validating the central role of expectations and exchange rate pass-through in a structurally fragile, import-dependent economy. The results suggest that sustainable price stability in Turkey hinges on reestablishing central bank independence, adopting orthodox inflation targeting, and regaining public trust through consistent and transparent communication. Introduction Inflation is inherently complex, and this complexity contributes to persistent uncer- tainty regarding both its causes and the extent to which it can be explained. This issue is particularly acute in emerging markets, where the adverse economic and social effects of inflation are deeply felt (see Bick, 2010; Yilmazkuday, 2011, 2022). While many emerg- ing economies have managed to reduce inflation through sound monetary frameworks, Turkey continues to struggle with high and volatile inflation. As of 2024, Turkey holds the second-highest inflation rate among emerging markets after Argentina, marking a structural divergence from global trends. Understanding Turkey’s inflation dynamics requires a historical perspective, as price in- stability has been a recurring feature of the economy. From the early 1940s onward, Turkey’s J. The period from 1980 to 2001 was characterized by chronic high inflation and financial instability, despite market-oriented reforms. A signif- icant improvement came between 2002 and 2016, as inflation targeting and IMF-backed stabilization programs brought price stability (Arpac & Bird, 2009; Yeldan, 2011). However, beginning in 2017, heterodox monetary policies, declining central bank independence, and global shocks such as COVID-19 reignited inflationary pressures, leading to a resurgence of double-digit inflation. As of December 2024, the annual inflation rate stood at 44.38%. Accordingly, this study revisits the core determinants of inflation in Turkey by combining a monetarist theoretical foundation with a cutting-edge machine learning framework. The main objective is to re-evaluate inflation dynamics under the lens of Quantity- Theoretical Inflation Theory (QTIT) using a novel Composite Machine Learning Time Series Analysis (CMTSA) approach. Theoretical Background The results of implementing anti-inflationary policies in many countries worldwide, when analyzed over a sufficiently long period, largely confirm the quantity theory of inflation’s proposition that inflation is a monetary phenomenon (Grauwe & Polan, 2005; Focacci & Focacci, 2024). This is the basis of perhaps the most famous and often quoted statement by Friedman (1994, p. 49): “Inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phe- nomenon, in the sense that it is and can only be produced by a faster increase in the money supply than in output”. The vitality of this proposition lies in the ability of the equation of exchange to be applied, explicitly or implicitly, to ever-changing historical conditions and institutional changes. For Turkey, the co-movement of inflation is also significantly driven by the co-movement of monetary policy (Saygılı, 2023). Graff (2008) derived the quantity theory of inflation, which takes into account the percentage changes (or growth rates) over time of variables in the quantity theory of money. The theory incorporates price determination within the traditional model (Moser, 1995). Accordingly, the model is extended to account for both openness and expectations, thereby enabling an analysis of whether the source of inflation is monetary, cost-push, demand-pull, or structural. In this regard, the model offers a robust theoretical framework for understanding the multifaceted nature of inflation. Consequently, this section of the study derives an inflation function for Turkey based on the mathematical foundations of the quantity theory of inflation. As it is known, Turkey is a small economy that is open to the outside. In a small open economy, the general level of prices (P) is a weighted average of the prices of domestic goods (PD) and the prices of imported goods subject to foreign trade (PM). Data This study presents a Composite Machine Learning Time Series Analysis (CMTSA) framework to examine the dynamic relationships proposed by the Quantity-Theoretical Inflation Theory (QTIT) in Turkey using monthly data whose raw coverage extends from May 2003 to January 2025. The framework integrates advanced machine learning tools with traditional econometric techniques to capture both linear and nonlinear interactions among key macroeconomic variables. Because the models are estimated on rates of change and the expectations proxy requires lagged information, the initial months of the raw sample are consumed by these transformations, and the estimation dataset comprises 260 monthly observations spanning June 2003 to January 2025 across eight macroeconomic indicators, of which the price level is the modelling target and the remaining seven serve as predictors, covering critical episodes such as the 2008 global financial crisis, the 2018 Turkish currency crisis, and the post-COVID-19 economic shifts.

These properties reflect the intrinsically difficult task faced by policymakers in a small, open economy subject to significant variability, that relies heavily on imports, and that is subject to potential external shocks and policy regime changes. Formal structural break tests reported in Section Structural Break Tests confirm this instability. They date a significant break at the currency crisis of 2018M08 and place the dominant regime shift in late 2021. A remark on the choice of the exchange rate measure is in order. The analysis employs the bilateral nominal TL/USD rate rather than a real or trade-weighted effective index, and this choice follows directly from the theoretical model. Equation (2) defines the domestic price of imported goods as the product of the foreign price level and the nominal exchange rate, so the nominal bilateral rate is the variable that the derivation itself prescribes. A CPI-based real effective exchange rate would be unsuitable in this framework for a mechanical reason: its construction embeds the domestic consumer price index, which is the very variable the models seek to explain, and its inclusion would therefore introduce circularity between regressor and target. In addition, the TL/USD rate is the relevant pricing benchmark in the Turkish context, where import invoicing and financial dollarization are overwhelmingly denominated in US dollars, and the imported cost information that a currency basket would carry is already spanned jointly by the exchange rate (E) and the import price index (P*) that enter the models as separate predictors.

Structural Break Tests To formally substantiate the structural instability evident in Figures 2 and 3, we subject the series to a battery of structural break tests. First, we apply the multiple breakpoint procedure of Bai and Perron (1998, 2003) to the monthly inflation rate and to the rate of change of the nominal exchange rate. The procedure is based on least squares segmentation with a 15% trimming rule, and the number of breaks is selected by the Bayesian Information Criterion. Second, we compute Chow (1960) tests at three candidate break dates: the shift toward heterodox policies in 2017M01, the currency crisis in 2018M08, and the beginning of the unorthodox rate-cut cycle in 2021M11. These tests use an AR(1) specification for inflation. Third, we run the unit root test of Zivot and Andrews (1992), which allows for a single endogenously determined break. Finally, we inspect the CUSUM of squares statistic for variance stability. The results, reported in Table 3, formally confirm the presence of structural breaks and refine their timing. The Chow test rejects parameter stability at the currency crisis of 2018M08 with an F statistic of 15.13 and a p-value below 0.001, which corroborates the regime shift emphasized in the historical narrative. At the same time, all three endogenous dating procedures, namely the Bai and Perron segmentation, the Zivot and Andrews test, and the CUSUM of squares statistic, locate the dominant break in late 2021, between 2021M10 and 2021M11. At that point, the average monthly inflation rate rose roughly fivefold, from 0.81% to 4.15%. This date coincides with the unorthodox rate-cut cycle initiated in September 2021 and with the ensuing collapse of the lira in December 2021. Conclusions This study re-examined the determinants of inflation in Turkey using a comprehen- sive machine-learning-based approach rooted in the Quantity-Theoretical Inflation Theory (QTIT). By employing a Composite Machine Learning Time Series Analysis (CMTSA) framework—integrating Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), Random Forest algorithms, and the DoWhy causal inference toolkit—the study uncovers nuanced dynamics that conven- tional linear models often fail to detect. The findings of this research not only reaffirm monetarist perspectives on inflation but also provide novel insights into the role of non- linear interactions, regime shifts, and expectation-driven mechanisms in shaping inflation trajectories in an emerging market context. One of the central findings is that inflation expectations and the nominal exchange rate are the most powerful and consistent predictors of inflation in Turkey. This result is confirmed across all methodological pathways—DNN interpretability via SHAP, Random Forest feature importance, and DoWhy’s causal treatment effect estimates. The prominence of expectations aligns with behavioral macroeconomic theories and the New Keynesian Phillips Curve (NKPC), which emphasizes the forward-looking nature of price-setting behavior. In Turkey’s case, especially during the post-2017 heterodox policy period, weakened policy credibility and frequent shifts in the policy regime ap- pear to have unanchored expectations, amplifying inflation’s volatility and persistence. This expectation channel is further exacerbated by exchange rate instability, whereby lira depreciation rapidly translates into higher domestic prices through imported input costs and foreign currency-denominated liabilities. We state this claim with an appropriate qualification: the precise ranking of predictors is model dependent. The random forest attributes the largest built-in importance to the real interest rate, at 47.2%, whereas the SHAP attribution of the network and the causal estimates favor expectations and the exchange rate. What is robust across methods is therefore not a single ordering but the joint prominence of expectations and the exchange rate, and it is on this shared signal that our conclusions rest. However, their impact appears asymmetric and nonlinear; during some periods, especially under negative real interest rate regimes, they fail to suppress inflation expectations, likely due to diminished credibility of the policy stance. The causal analysis adds direct evidence on this point: the estimated effect of the real interest rate on inflation is negative and statistically significant (−0.213 in robust scaled units), which confirms that positive real returns restrain price growth. Nevertheless, the impact of oil prices becomes more salient when considered through indirect channels—mainly exchange rates and expectations. In a highly import-dependent and energy-insecure economy like Turkey’s, the pass-through of global cost shocks to domestic inflation depends on currency valuation and the overall monetary policy stance. Hence, even though the conditional statistical contribution of oil prices appears marginal, their economic relevance cannot be dismissed, particularly in an open economy context. However, the integration of machine learning reveals more intricate dynamics. For instance, expectations are often treated as residual components in structural VAR models or omitted entirely in traditional analyses due to data limitations. In contrast, this study explic- itly and rigorously quantifies their causal power. Moreover, by identifying the feedback loops between expectations, monetary policy instruments, and inflation, it contributes to the grow- ing literature on credibility and central bank communication in inflation-targeting regimes. From a policy perspective, the findings of this research have several important im- plications. First and foremost, restoring the credibility of monetary policy must be a top priority. Inflation expectations are found to be the strongest causal driver of actual in- flation; as such, credible forward guidance and consistent policy actions are vital. This requires re-establishing central bank independence, refraining from political interference, and transparently communicating the monetary policy stance to the public. Second, policy normalization toward orthodox frameworks—particularly inflation target- ing with positive real interest rates—is essential. The study clearly demonstrates that negative real interest rates, combined with rapid money supply growth, have led to inflationary spirals. Reinstating real returns on lira-denominated assets would help anchor expectations, stabilize capital flows, and support currency valuation, thereby reducing imported inflation. Third, exchange rate management should be an integral part of inflation control. Although a floating exchange rate regime is theoretically desirable, in the context of shallow financial markets and high dollarization, passive currency depreciation feeds inflation through both expectations and import channels. Although not the primary focus of this study, the historical context reveals that inflationary episodes in Turkey have often been associated with fiscal dominance and monetization of debt. Strengthening fiscal discipline and reducing quasi-fiscal expenditures can help alleviate the inflationary burden on monetary authorities. Fifth, improved data transparency and monitoring of inflation expectations are needed. Currently, expectations are proxied using backward-looking indicators due to the limited availability of survey-based or market-implied measures. Developing such tools can enhance real-time policy evaluation and guide better decision-making. Finally, for future researchers, this study opens several pathways. Incorporating real- time data and forward-looking variables such as inflation-indexed bond yields or consumer surveys could improve expectation modeling. Additionally, extending the CMTSA frame- work to include geopolitical risks, supply chain disruptions, or political uncertainty indices may offer a more holistic view of inflation dynamics. Sectoral disaggregation—such as analyzing inflation in tradable vs. non-tradable sectors—could also reveal the distribu- tional impact of monetary policy. Comparative studies using similar frameworks in other emerging markets may further validate the generalizability of these findings and refine our understanding of inflation under varying institutional conditions. A further natural extension is to replicate the framework with alternative exchange rate measures, such as the nominal effective rate or a trade-weighted basket, in order to verify that the dominance of the exchange rate channel does not hinge on the bilateral TL/USD definition adopted here on theoretical grounds. In conclusion, this research demonstrates that advanced analytical methods can mean- ingfully contribute to macroeconomic policy formulation, particularly in complex, high- volatility environments. Turkey’s inflation story is not simply about monetary expansion or external shocks, but about the interplay of expectations, credibility, and institutional integrity. Addressing inflation sustainably thus requires a holistic approach—grounded in empirical rigor, theoretical clarity, and consistent policy action.
